Freehold ground-floor retail unit on Lorong Kilat in Beauty World for sale at $8.5 mil
article:
A first-floor strata retail unit at Sun Court , a residential development on Lorong Kilat in the Beauty World area, is up for sale through an expression of interest (EOI) exercise. The freehold unit has a guide price of $8.5 million, or $3,495 psf on its strata area of 2,432 sq ft.

The unit is approved for restaurant use and is currently tenanted, according to marketing agent Huttons Asia. “At approximately 2,432 sq ft, this freehold ground-floor unit offers the scale that many operators look for when planning a more substantial dining concept,” added Yeo Khee Liang, associate senior marketing director at Huttons.

Sun Court is a freehold apartment block at 21 Lorong Kilat with retail units on the ground floor. Completed in 1985, it has less than 20 residences. It is part of a row of similar low-rise developments on Lorong Kilat, about a five-minute walk away from the Beauty World MRT Station on the Downtown line.

Retail shops at the developments serve the surrounding Beauty World and Bukit Timah residential enclaves, included the nearby landed housing estates off Jalan Jurong Kechil and Upper Bukit Timah Road .

“Retail spaces in Lorong Kilat are seldom put up for sale,” said Lee Sze Teck, senior director of data analytics at Huttons.

Lodged caveats show just one transaction for a Lorong Kilat commercial unit in the past five years. A freehold strata shop at Sun Court changed hands for $2.05 million in June 2021, which works out to $1,380 psf on its 1,485 sq ft strata area.

The EOI will close at 3pm on Nov 24.

title: 3 SGX Dividend Stocks to Watch as the STI Dips
article:
Falling markets have a way of making every
dividend
look like a bargain.
The
Straits Times Index
(SGX: ^STI) has now slipped more than 7.3% from its all-time high.
It’s tempting to reach for the biggest payouts on offer.
A lower share price does nothing to protect a dividend, though.
Cash does.
So before you buy, ask how a company pays for what it hands you.
The three SGX companies below all
raised their dividends
in the first half of 2026 (1H2026), though each one funded its payout in its own way.

Note: Yield figures are as at 27 October 2026. (Source: Fiscal.ai)
Can Union Gas keep paying more as it adds stations?
Union Gas Holdings Limited
(SGX: 1F2) distributes gas fuels and runs Cnergy service stations.
Its profit attributable to shareholders rose 175.8% year on year (YoY) to S$12 million.
The board could have lifted the regular dividend to match.
It didn’t; instead, it held the interim dividend steady and paid a special dividend instead:
Interim dividend: S$0.0048 per share, unchanged from a year ago
Special dividend: S$0.0032 per share, the group’s first
Total dividends rose 66.7% YoY to S$0.008 per share.
All of that increase came from the special, so don’t count on it every year.
The cash backs it up.
Free cash flow climbed to S$25.1 million, up from just S$1.3 million a year ago, helping the group maintain a healthy net cash position of S$21.7 million as at 30 June 2026.
The growth was largely driven by its service station network, where total revenue rose 66.4% to S$105.9 million.
Liquid fuel revenue jumped 444.4% to S$51.7 million as new stations at Dunman Road and Queensway began contributing.
Growth won’t come free.
Stations in Marsiling and Jurong West are due to open in 2027, and the group spent S$8.2 million buying two LPG retailers on 31 July 2026.
Related articles:
Forget the Blue Chips: 4 SGX Stocks Quietly Outperforming the STI
3 SGX Hidden Gems Surprising Investors with Bonus Dividends
Is Nanofilm’s bigger dividend backed by lasting cash flow?
Nanofilm Technologies International Limited
(SGX: MZH) makes advanced materials coatings and nanofabricated products.
It doubled its interim dividend to S$0.006 per share on the back of a 65.6% YoY surge in net profit to S$4.3 million.
While that percentage jump looks impressive, it comes off a relatively small base from the prior period.
Cash flow told a bigger story.
Free cash flow turned positive at S$19.5 million, up from an outflow of S$10.3 million from the previous year.
Free cash flow is the lifeblood of dividends, and here it ran far ahead of profit.
Part of that gap came from customers paying what they already owed, but don’t expect that boost every half.
Revenue grew 6.1% to S$113.7 million, but the more lasting change shows up in margins.
Gross margin widened to 38.6% from 32.6% as automation and cost discipline lifted productivity.
Research and engineering expenses also rose 56.6%.
Much of that reflects accounting, not extra spending: as projects moved into production, less of the cost was set aside to be expensed in later years.
Total R&D spending actually fell to S$17.4 million from S$19.1 million.
Cash of S$88.7 million roughly matched total bank borrowings of S$88.8 million as at 30 June 2026.
The second half of the year will test the recovery.
Management expects stronger equipment deliveries in 2H2026, helped by its order backlog.
Conversely, tighter memory chip supply and rising component prices may squeeze margins.
Related articles:
Beyond Blue Chips: 3 SGX Stocks Quietly Buying Back Their Own Shares
Top 3 Small-Cap Stocks Big Money Is Buying in April 2026
What does ValueMax’s borrowing mean for its dividend?
ValueMax Group Limited
(SGX: T6I) runs pawnbroking and secured moneylending businesses, and retails and trades gold and jewellery.
It raised its interim dividend 15% YoY to S$0.0138 per share, which was paid out on 3 September 2026.
Net profit attributable to shareholders increased 30.4% to S$62.6 million, giving the dividend hike plenty of cover relative to earnings growth.
Revenue rose 38.2% to S$370.7 million, though gross margin narrowed to 27.0% from 30.2% as lower-margin gold sales made up more of the mix.
Here’s the thing: ValueMax lends money for a living, so its cash flow looks different.
Free cash flow came in at negative S$34.1 million, compared to negative S$14.5 million a year earlier, as trade and other receivables absorbed S$192.7 million to fund loan book expansion.
For a financial lender, growing the loan book builds future earnings power, but it naturally consumes cash upfront.
That growth leans on borrowing.
Total borrowings, excluding lease liabilities, reached S$1.05 billion as at 30 June 2026, up 18.1% over six months, against cash and bank balances of S$18.8 million.
That debt is why ValueMax is the most nuanced case of the three.
Management expects gold prices to stay volatile after peaking near US$5,300 an ounce in March 2026, and it has flagged rising competition.
Get Smart: Trace the cash before you buy the dip
A
falling share price
tells you nothing about whether a payout will last.
So follow the money.
Start by separating any special dividend from the ordinary payout, as Union Gas shows.
Then ask whether free cash flow came from the business or from collecting old receivables.
Nanofilm’s latest half had a bit of both.
And at ValueMax, borrowing pays for growth, so keep an eye on that debt.
The STI’s dip lets you buy dividend payers at lower prices.
Just make sure you pick the ones whose cash you understand.

title: Dongshan precision slips in debut after US$1.3 bil HK listing
article:
(Oct 28): Suzhou Dongshan Precision Manufacturing Co shares slumped on their first day of trading in Hong Kong after the company raised HK$9.9 billion (US$1.3 billion or $1.6 billion), a debut that tests investor appetite for artificial intelligence (AI)-linked listings after a sharp market pullback.

The printed circuit board maker’s stock declined as much as 6.1% early Wednesday, after the company priced 113.8 million shares at HK$86.80 apiece, below the maximum and at a 35% discount to the previous close of its Shenzhen-listed stock. The deal was about half the size of the US$3 billion ($3.9 billion) Dongshan first sought and gave Dongshan Precision a market value of about US$30 billion.

The debut arrives at a tricky moment for Hong Kong. A listing boom has put the 2021 record in share-sale proceeds within reach, but rising bond yields and poor deal performance have made investors and issuers turn more cautious recently. A string of initial public offering withdrawals and delays, including by major data centre operators in the region, has also added pressure that’s prompted some companies in Hong Kong to put near-term listing plans on hold.

“It still looks more like a falling knife, particularly as investors reassess AI-related valuations and spending,” said Gerald Gan, chief investment officer at Singapore-based Reed Capital. The decision to cut the Hong Kong offering from as much as US$3 billion “also tells me that appetite for large deals is becoming more selective — Hong Kong’s IPO pipeline remains active, but investors are increasingly demanding better valuations rather than buying every AI-related listing indiscriminately”.

Dongshan’s was the 10th Hong Kong listing this year to top US$1 billion in proceeds, out of almost 120 deals so far, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. The biggest were Zhongji Innolight Co and Luxshare Precision Industry Co, which raised US$7.8 billion and US$3.2 billion, respectively. That’s the most billion-dollar listings since 2020, when there were 16.

See also: Anthropic IPO filing calms nerves with signs of healthy growth

The blowout year has been driven in large part by Chinese companies along the AI supply chain. Other PCB makers with recent listings include Victory Giant Technology Huizhou Co, which raised US$3 billion in one of Hong Kong’s biggest deals of the year, and Shenzhen Kinwong Electronic Co, which completed a US$650 million debut in September.

Cornerstone investors — which get guaranteed allocation in the deal in exchange for holding the stock for at least six months — including JPMorgan Asset Management, Alibaba Group Holding Ltd, CPE and Montage Technology Co, agreed to buy a combined 50% of the offering. Jane Street Group and Jump Trading LLC are also among them.

The Suzhou-based company makes PCBs and optical transceivers, key components for AI. It’s the third-largest PCB supplier in an US$85.2 billion global market, according to its filing.

See also: Acts of God meet acts of AI in private equity’s new debt play

UBS Group AG, Guotai Haitong Securities Co, GF Securities Co and Citic Securities Co are joint sponsors for the Hong Kong listing, according to the preliminary prospectus.

title: Chinese EV imports surge in Thailand ahead of planned excise tax
article:
(Oct 28): Thailand’s imports of electric passenger cars more than doubled in September, almost entirely driven by China, as booming demand and the prospect of higher taxes on fully imported EVs lifted shipments.

Imports surged 138% from a year earlier to US$421 million, with China supplying almost 99% of the total, government data showed. The value was also 86% higher than in August. In the first nine months of the year, Thailand imported US$2.37 billion of electric passenger cars, 96% of them from China.

The surge highlights the challenge Thailand is trying to address with higher taxes on imported EVs. After decades building Southeast Asia’s biggest auto-manufacturing hub, the government wants booming electric-car demand to translate into local production and jobs rather than a growing dependence on vehicles shipped from China.

Thailand is now considering an excise tax of around 30% on fully imported EVs as part of a new structure designed to favor domestic manufacturing. Finance Minister Ekniti Nitithanprapas has said the government is working with automakers to finalise the rate.

A three-tier structure approved in principle by Thailand’s EV policy board in September would impose the highest excise tax on fully imported vehicles, a lower rate on cars assembled locally with imported components and the lowest on EVs with greater domestic production and content.

See also: Universal Music discussed going private with buyout firms

The prospect of higher taxes may already be pulling some imports forward. Nantapong Chiralerspong, director-general of the Trade Policy and Strategy Office, said September’s surge reflected both strong demand and the expansion of Chinese EV brands, with anticipation of the proposed tax potentially accelerating shipments.

The surge comes alongside rapid growth in the domestic EV market. Sales of battery-electric passenger cars jumped 80% from a year earlier to 16,404 in September and nearly doubled to 161,532 in the first nine months, according to the Federation of Thai Industries.

The industry expects that momentum to continue. New EV registrations are forecast to reach 200,000 to 220,000 this year, up from about 120,000 in 2025, according to Surapong Paisitpatnapong, an adviser to the Federation of Thai Industries chairman and spokesman for its Automotive Industry Club. Registrations had already reached 165,040 through September.

title: Anthropic said to pick JPMorgan to lead IPO’s US retail offering — Bloomberg
article:
(Oct 28): Anthropic PBC has tapped JPMorgan Chase & Co to lead US sales of shares to individual investors in its potentially record-setting initial public offering, people familiar with the matter said.

The company behind Claude has weighed a retail offering of about 15% to 20% of the shares available in the IPO overall, some of the people said. JPMorgan chief executive officer Jamie Dimon is expected to take part in the Wall Street bank’s campaign, one of them added.

JPMorgan is reprising its role leading the effort to gather retail orders for SpaceX’s US$86.2 billion IPO, which saw more than US$100 billion of demand from individual investors, Bloomberg News has reported.

Citigroup Inc. is set to coordinate the international retail offering, some of the people said, asking not to be identified as the information isn’t public. Anthropic’s IPO includes offerings in Australia, Canada, Japan, certain European Economic Area countries, Switzerland and the UK, according to the IPO filing.

JPMorgan is coordinating outreach on Anthropic’s IPO to high-net-worth investors and private banking clients, as well as broker platforms, the people said.

Deliberations are ongoing and details including the share of the offering earmarked for retail could change, the people said. Representatives for Anthropic, JPMorgan and Citigroup declined to comment.

Anthropic filed publicly on Monday for an IPO that would see it and some of its investors sell shares, marking the first listing by a company focused primarily on developing the most advanced AI models. Goldman Sachs Group Inc and Morgan Stanley are leading the offering.

Investors are telling bankers on the deal that their estimate of a fair valuation has shifted to around US$1.4 trillion to US$1.5 trillion, though a valuation of closer to US$1.75 trillion is potentially achievable, Bloomberg News has reported.

The amount of money needed to fund the development of AI and its associated infrastructure has spurred companies to raise tens of billions of dollars at a time.

See also: Dubai firm’s US$543 mil IPO covered within minutes despite war

Meta Platforms Inc on Monday kicked off a plan to raise as much as US$98 billion in equity, which would be one of the largest financing exercises of its kind in history. It follows Google parent Alphabet Inc’s US$85 billion equity fundraising plan earlier this year.

Anthropic and rival OpenAI are seeking to raise record amounts while facing mounting public scrutiny over AI safety after a string of high-profile hacking incidents by rogue agents.

title: Seatrium and Karpowership explore JV for floating power solutions in Singapore
article:
Mainboard-listed Seatrium has signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with Turkish energy company Karpowership to pursue a joint venture to develop floating power and infrastructure solutions in Singapore.

The partnership was announced at Singapore International Energy Week on Oct 27 and was witnessed by Tan See Leng, Singapore’s Minister for Energy, Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry).

Under the MoU, the two companies plan to create an integrated platform combining infrastructure development, financing, engineering, construction and operations. It also establishes a framework to jointly develop rapidly deployable power and infrastructure solutions in Singapore, which may include Powerships, floating data centres, turbine-based or hybrid vessels and floating nuclear solutions.

Across Southeast Asia, the similar growth of digital industries has also led to increased infrastructure requirements. According to the 9th ASEAN Energy Outlook, 20% of ASEAN's projected electricity demand growth in the next five years will be attributable to data centres. Coupled with structural drivers of industrialisation and urbanisation, generation capacity for reliable power to support industrial activity and other energy-intensive facilities is crucial.

Against this backdrop, floating power infrastructure could provide additional options to enhance supply security, including through the rapid deployment of generation capacity, contingency power provision and support for critical infrastructure, including data centres. Such solutions could also offer flexibility in deployment locations, enable power generation assets to be adapted or redeployed, and chart a longer-term transition pathway as energy requirements continue to evolve.

Seatrium CEO Chris Ong says that Seatrium’s offshore engineering heritage, systems integration capabilities and advanced facilities in Singapore provide a strong foundation to strengthen Singapore’s status as a hub for next-generation floating energy and digital infrastructure, supporting domestic needs and opportunities across the region.

See also: Singapore’s EMA backs grid resilience projects with $14.9 mil

“As demand for power and digital infrastructure accelerates, our industry has an opportunity to develop new solutions that combine speed of deployment, flexibility and scale,”remarks Ong. “For Seatrium, this represents a strategic opportunity to extend our role across the energy infrastructure value chain, creating new avenues for growth where we can apply our proven capabilities to shape critical infrastructure that underpin the region’s future competitiveness.”

Karpowership CEO Orhan Remzi Karadeniz says that the firm’s decades-long relationships with OEMs and technology partners, including Seatrium and hyperscalers, position Karpowership as a go-to provider of integrated infrastructure solutions at pace and scale.

“Together with Seatrium, our ambition is to build an integrated platform in Singapore that brings development, financing, engineering and operations together to deliver power where and when it is needed, strengthening energy security and enabling growth across Southeast Asia,” says Karadeniz.

See also: Sembcorp and ST Engineering prepare for nuclear future

Shares in Seatrium closed flat at $1.82 on Oct 27.

title: DBS sees nuclear opportunities
article:
To seize money-making opportunities in financing nuclear energy projects presumably, banks have to build up the capability and knowledge in the subject to be part of the nuclear power ecosystem, suggests Ganesh Padmanabhan, managing director and head of project finance at DBS, Singapore’s largest and most profitable bank.

Speaking at a Singapore International Energy Week panel on Oct 27, Padmanabhan shares that due to various reasons including regulations and project size and scale, nuclear power is “beyond the reach” of commercial bank funding. “From a financing standpoint, historically, nuclear hasn't had commercial bank financing at all,” he says. “There's no track record.”

Because commercial banks have not had a need to consider nuclear opportunities, they have not developed the expertise to evaluate such projects. However, with the emergence of small modular reactors (SMRs) which are smaller and less costly, banks may have the opportunity to finance nuclear power, mentions Padmanabhan.

“I think the banks also have to build that capability and that knowledge to be able to walk alongside the developers, the regulators, and other stakeholders in this area,” says Padmanabhan. Presumably, with expertise in nuclear, banks would be able to evaluate risks and opportunities in nuclear power projects.

He also suggests other considerations including risk diversification among stakeholders. “So to me, I think covering risk elements through support from the government, be it in the form of some kind of a regulatory asset, a PPP [public-private partnership] model, or even bringing an export credit agency into supporting these, will make it a bit more bankable to bring in commercial banks into the financing mix itself,” remarks Padmanabhan.

While Singapore has not yet made a decision on adopting nuclear energy, it is aggressively preparing itself for such a possibility with a raft of initiatives in recent months. These include announcing talent development programmes in nuclear and collaborations with other countries on knowledge sharing and research.

On the commercial front, Mainboard-listed Sembcorp Industries and ST Engineering will be collaborating to prepare themselves for nuclear energy. Sembcorp will also partner Canadian nuclear engineering firm AtkinsRéalis to “explore collaboration opportunities” in the nuclear energy sector.

Overall, Singapore is building capabilities across 19 key areas identified by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) as necessary for a country to establish a nuclear power programme. Areas include funding and financing, industrial involvement, nuclear safety and radioactive waste management, among others.

Furthermore, to assess its readiness and ensure these capability building efforts are advancing in the right direction, Singapore has embarked on the Integrated Nuclear Infrastructure Review (INIR) conducted by the IAEA.

Speaking at the same panel, Kim Han Gon, president of the Innovative Small Modular Reactor (i-SMR) Development Agency, says that financial risk associated with a first-of-its-kind project is a hurdle hindering SMR commercialisation. “This [financial] risk is particularly significant when the full project relies on private investment, so our approach is to reduce this financial risk step by step,” he adds.

The i-SMR Development Agency is a South Korean government-backed organisation established to lead the development and commercialisation of the country's homegrown i-SMR.

With government backing and collaborations with Korea Hydro and Nuclear Power (KHNP) and Korea Electric Power Corporation (KEPCO), Kim says the agency aims to de-risk first deployment. He expects that a successful i-SMR project will provide reference design and clear evidence on the construction costs, schedule, and performance. “This experience will make subsequent projects easier for private investment,” he states.

He sees opportunities for different forms of private participation at different stages. “Industrial partners may participate in the projects, because of their technical capability and their long-term business interests [while] broader private investment can then expand as the technology and delivery model becomes more established,” he says. “Our goal is to reduce the risk, but it does not mean that we can guarantee that investors will never lose money.”

Shares in DBS closed at $73.92 on Oct 27. Ytd, the counter is up by more than 30%.
